# THE PRINCIPLES
# OF PHILOSOPHY
### The Most Ancient and Most Modern
#### CONCERNING
### GOD, CHRIST, AND THE CREATURE
#### that is
### Concerning Spirit and Matter in general.

> *By the benefit of which all problems can be resolved, which could be resolved neither by Scholastic Philosophy <note>The traditional system of theology and philosophy taught in medieval European universities, based on Aristotelian logic.</note>, nor by the common modern philosophy, nor by the **CARTESIAN**, **HOBBESIAN**, or **SPINOZISTIC** philosophies <note>References to René Descartes, Thomas Hobbes, and Baruch Spinoza, the dominant "modern" thinkers of the 17th century whom the author seeks to challenge or transcend.</note>.*

### A Posthumous Small Work
### Translated from the English Language into Latin with Annotations drawn from the ancient philosophy of the Hebrews <note>original: "ex antiqua Hebræorum Philosophia" - This refers to the Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism that the author synthesized with Christian thought.</note>.

# TO THE
# READER.

### TO THE KIND READER.

*This little work we publish for your sake, which was written not so many years ago by a certain English Countess* <note>The author is Lady Anne Conway (1631–1679), a philosopher who corresponded with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz and Henry More.</note>*, a woman learned beyond her sex, most skilled in Latin and Greek literature, and most thoroughly experienced in every kind of philosophizing. When she had first been imbued with the principles of Descartes* <note>original: Cartesii; referring to René Descartes, the famous French philosopher.</note>*, and having seen their defects, she afterwards observed so many things from the reading of certain writers of the genuine Philosophy of Antiquity* <note>This likely refers to her studies in Neoplatonism and the Kabbalah.</note> *that she wrote these few chapters for her own use, but only in pencil* <note>original: plumbagine</note> *and in a very tiny handwriting. Which, when they were found after her death, were partially transcribed (because those things which remain could hardly be read up until now) and were translated into Latin* <note>original: Latinitate donata; the work was originally written in English, translated into Latin for this 1690 edition, and the original English manuscript is now lost.</note>*, so that from this...*

<meta>The text on this page ends mid-sentence; the preface continues on the following page.</meta>

<summary>This preface introduces Anne Conway as an exceptionally learned English Countess who, after moving beyond Cartesianism, wrote a private philosophical treatise in a small, penciled hand. The text explains that these notes were recovered after her death and translated into Latin for publication.</summary>

<keywords>Anne Conway, René Descartes, Philosophy of Antiquity, Latin translation, 17th-century philosophy, female philosophers</keywords>

...utility might come to the whole learned world <note>original: "orbi literato"; this refers to the "Republic of Letters," the international community of scholars and intellectuals who used Latin as a shared language during the 17th century.</note>. 

And these same writings are now made public <note>original: "publici juris"; a Latin legal phrase meaning the work is now published and available for everyone to read, rather than being kept in private manuscript form.</note>, so that anyone might be able to admire the Author, recognize true Philosophy <margin>+</margin>, and more easily avoid those errors which—alas!—are now all too common. May you enjoy these, and farewell <note>original: "Vale"; a standard Latin closing for a letter or preface, literally meaning "be well."</note>.

# PRINCIPLES
# OF PHILOSOPHY
### Most Ancient and Most Modern
### CONCERNING
## GOD, CHRIST, AND THE CREATURE
<note>original: "Creatura"; in 17th-century philosophy, "the Creature" refers to the totality of created existence—all things brought into being by God—rather than a single living thing.</note>
->THAT IS<-
### *Concerning Spirit and Matter in general.*

---

## CHAPTER I.
## CONCERNING GOD AND HIS DIVINE ATTRIBUTES.

§ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. *Concerning GOD and his divine attributes.* § 6, 7. *In what way the Trinity can be conceived of in GOD according to Scripture so that Jews, Turks <note>original: "Turcae"; in the 17th century, this term was commonly used to refer to Muslims and the Ottoman world at large.</note>, or any other people might not be offended, if these terms—"Three distinct persons"—which are neither found in Scripture nor have a sound meaning, are omitted.*

§ I. **G**OD is Spirit, light, and life; infinitely wise, good, just, strong, all-knowing, all-present, and all-powerful; the Creator and maker of all things visible and invisible. See, Sketch— <note>original: "Vid. Adumbra-"; this is an abbreviation for "Vide Adumbratio," likely referring to a related work or a specific section titled "A Sketch." The catchword "bra." at the bottom of the page confirms the word is "Adumbratio."</note>

<summary>This is the title page and the beginning of Chapter I of Anne Conway’s philosophical work, defining God as an infinite, all-powerful Spirit and proposing a way to discuss the Trinity without using non-scriptural terms that might alienate non-Christians.</summary>

Through this Idea, He knows Himself no less than He knows all other things; and according to this—indeed, through this very Idea or Word—all creatures were made and created.

§ 7. By the same reasoning, there is in God a Spirit or Will, which proceeds from Him, and yet as far as substance and essence are concerned, is one with Him. Through this, Creatures receive their essence and activity, because Creatures have their essence and existence simply from this: because God wills them to be. He is Will according to knowledge, which is most infinite. And thus Wisdom and Will in God are not some Entity <term>Entity (Entitas): A distinct being or thing with its own independent existence.</term> or substance distinct from Him, but rather distinct modes or properties of one and the same

And since this is the very thing that those among Christians who excel most in knowledge and judgment understand by the Trinity: if that phrase regarding "three distinct persons" were now set aside—which is a stumbling block <note>original: "lapis offensionis"; a biblical idiom referring to something that causes someone to trip or take offense.</note> both to the Jews and to the Turks <note>In the 17th century, "Turks" was a common term for Muslims.</note>, and to other peoples, and which in itself does not truly have a sound meaning, nor is it found anywhere in scripture—everyone could then easily agree on this article of faith. For they by no means deny that God possesses wisdom, an Essential Idea, and such a Word <note>original: "verbum"</note> within Himself according to which He knows all things. And since they concede that the same [God] gives essence to all things, they are also necessarily compelled to acknowledge that there is in Him a Will, through which He carries out and brings into action what is hidden in that Idea; namely, so that He may produce it and from there make a distinct Essential substance. And this is the very act of creating—namely, the essence of the creature—for it is not the Idea alone that bestows being <term>Entity (Entitas): The state of being or having existence.</term> upon the Creature, but rather the Will joined with the Idea. Just as when an Architect has the Idea of a house in his mind, he does not build the house by the Idea alone, but the Will is joined to it and works together with it.

### *Notes on this first Chapter.*

## The ancient Hypothesis of the Hebrews, regarding the further contents of this chapter, is as follows:

1. Since **G**od was the most intense and indeed infinite light, and yet also the highest Goodness; for the sake of this goodness, He wished to establish Creatures to whom He might communicate Himself: yet these could by no means have endured His most intense light. And to this pertain those sayings of scripture: *God dwells in inaccessible light* <note>original: "Deus habitat in luce inaccessibili"; see 1 Timothy 6:16.</note>. *No one has ever seen God* <note>original: "Deum nemo vidit unquam"; see John 1:18.</note>, etc.

2. Therefore, for the sake of the Creatures (so that there might be a place for them), He diminished <note>This describes the Kabbalistic concept of Tzimtzum, or "contraction," where God creates a "space" for creation by withdrawing His infinite presence.</note> that highest degree of His intense light, from which a place arose—as if a circular vacuum—to serve as the space for the Worlds.

3. This vacuum was not a privation, or non-being; but a real placement of diminished light, which was the **Soul of the Messiah**, called <term>Primordial Man (Adam Kadmon: In Kabbalah, the first and highest stage of divine emanation, representing the divine plan for humanity)</term> by the Hebrews: by which that whole space was filled.

4 This soul of the Messiah was united with all that Light of Divinity which had remained within that vacuum at a gentler degree—one that could be endured—and together with it, it constituted one single subject.

<summary>This page outlines a Kabbalistic theory of creation, explaining how God diminished His infinite light to create a "vacuum" for the universe, which was then filled by the "Soul of the Messiah" or "Primordial Man."</summary>
<keywords>Adam Kadmon, Soul of the Messiah, divine light, Tzimtzum, creation, Hebrew hypothesis, Kabbalah, contraction</keywords>

<page-num>6</page-num>
<meta>catchword: CHAPTER.</meta>

5. This <term>Messias</term> (called the <term>Word (Logos: From the Greek logos, meaning "word" or "reason," often used in theology to describe the Divine expression or the second person of the Trinity)</term> or the Word and the firstborn son of God) established from within himself—by making a further lessening of his own light for the benefit of the Creatures—the sequence of all created things.

6. To these creatures, he further communicated the Lights of his Divinity and of his own nature, as objects of contemplation and love. These were the unifying acts between the Creatures and the Creator; the happiness of the creatures consisted in this union.

7. Therefore, a <term>Trinity</term> of Divine representation presents itself here: the first concept is God himself as the Infinite, considered outside and above the act of production; the second is the same God, insofar as he is in the Messiah; and the third is the same God, insofar as he is with the Messiah within the Creatures, at the lowest degree of light adapted for the perception of the Creatures. To this pertains that saying of Scripture:

> No one has ever seen God; (1) the Son (2) who is in the bosom of the Father (1) has made him known (3) to us (3). <note>original: "Deum nemo vidit unquam, Filius qui in sinu Patris est, nobis annunciavit"; see John 1:18. The numbers (1, 2, 3) in the text correspond to the three aspects of the Trinity defined in point 7.</note>

8. But it is also customary among the <term>Hebrews</term> to use the term "Persons," though in such a way that for them, "person" does not signify a single individual substance, but rather a concept, a form of representation, or a way of viewing God. [ *See the Sketch of the Christian Kabbalah, chapters 2 and 3.* <note>original: "Adumbratio Kabbalæ Christianæ"; this refers to a foundational text of Christian Kabbalah often attributed to Franciscus Mercurius van Helmont or Christian Knorr von Rosenroth.</note> ]

<summary>This page describes the Messiah as the Word and firstborn of God who creates the world by further dimming his divine light. It reinterprets the Christian Trinity as three modes of God's presence: as the Infinite, as the Messiah, and as a presence within all creatures.</summary>

# CHAPTER II.

§. 1. *Creatures, although they are not co-eternal with God, have nevertheless possessed infinite times from the beginning.* <note>The author is proposing a middle ground: the world has a "beginning" (it is not God), but that beginning is so distant it constitutes "infinite time."</note> §. 2. *So that no number of years—not even the greatest that a created intellect can conceive—can reach back to their very beginning.* §. 3. *Creatures, in a different sense, both were and were not from eternity.* §. 4. *The infinity of times is proved by the infinite goodness of GOD.* §. 5. *It is an essential ~~attribute~~ of GOD to be the Creator.* §. 6. *What time is, and for what reason it does not exist in GOD.*

---

§ 1. **A**nd since all creatures exist simply because of him alone, or exist because God wills them to be—whose will is infinitely powerful, and whose command (without any instrument, instrumental cause, or matter) is the sole <term>efficient cause (The primary source or agent that brings something into being)</term> for giving <term>being (original: "entitatem," referring to the quality of existing as a distinct entity)</term> to creatures—hence it necessarily follows that since the will of God is eternal (or exists from eternity), the act of creation follows that same will immediately and without any intervention of time. And although it cannot be said that creatures, considered in themselves, are [co-eternal] with God...

<summary>This page introduces the argument that the universe has existed for an infinite span of time because God’s eternal will acts immediately to create, making the age of the world beyond human calculation.</summary>
<keywords>creation, eternity, divine will, efficient cause, nature of time, infinite goodness, cosmology</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from page 7, where the author began explaining that although the creation has a beginning in God's will, that beginning is so deeply rooted in God's eternal nature that the universe must be far older than traditional chronologies suggest. The catchword "se" from the previous page correctly connects to the first word "se" here.</meta>

<page-num>8</page-num>

themselves <note>original: "se"</note> to be co-eternal, because by this reasoning eternity and time would be confused together. Nevertheless, creatures and that will which created them are so present to one another, and touch one another so immediately, that nothing can come between them, just as if two circles were touching each other immediately. Nor can we assign any other beginning to Creatures except God himself, and his eternal will, which is according to his eternal idea or wisdom. From this it follows by natural consequence that the times since Creation are infinite, and beyond any number that a <term>created intellect (a mind that is itself a part of creation, such as a human or an angel)</term> can conceive; for how can that be finite or measured which had no other beginning than eternity itself?

§. 2. If, however, someone should wish to say that times are finite, let us now suppose their measure from the beginning to be about 6,000 years <note>This refers to the common 17th-century belief, based on Biblical genealogies, that the Earth was roughly 6,000 years old.</note> (as some believe that the passage of time from the origin is no longer than this); or with others (who think that before this world there was another <term>invisible world (a spiritual or conceptual realm that preceded the physical universe)</term>, from which this <term>visible world (the physical universe we inhabit)</term> proceeded) let us suppose the duration of the world was 600,000 years, or any other number, even the largest, that can be conceived by any reasoning; I now ask whether it could have happened that the world was created earlier or before this time? If they deny the <term>power of God (original: "potentiam Dei")</term> to a certain number of years...

<summary>The author argues that because God's eternal will is the immediate cause of creation, the universe must have existed for a span of time so vast it is effectively infinite to the human mind. He challenges the traditional view that the world is only 6,000 years old, suggesting God's creative power could not be so limited.</summary>

<keywords>eternity, time, creation, will of God, infinite time, chronology, visible world, invisible world, divine power</keywords>

...restrict it, if they affirm this, they admit a time before all times, which is a manifest contradiction. <note>The author is arguing that if you say the world began at a specific point in time, you imply there was a "time" before that beginning, which is logically impossible if time is a property of the world itself.</note>

§. 3. These things having been established in the aforementioned way, it will now be easy to answer that question which has so greatly tormented many: whether Creation was made, or could have been made, from eternity, or from the eternal? <note>original: "ab æternitate, sive ab æterno"</note> For if by <term>eternity (an existence outside of time)</term> and the eternal they understand an infinite number of times, in this sense certainly creation was made from the eternal. He is the **First Mover** <term>primus motor: A philosophical term, rooted in Aristotelian thought, referring to the initial cause of all motion in the universe who remains unmoved and unchanged.</term> in all His creatures, according to all their true and ordered motions. He himself, however, is not moved by these; rather, that which corresponds analogically in Him to the motions or operations of creatures is the governance of His will. If we wish to speak precisely, this is not "motion," because all motion is **successive** <note>original: "motio successiva". This refers to movement that happens step-by-step through time, whereas God's act is viewed as eternal and simultaneous.</note>, and such a thing cannot take place in God, as has been demonstrated above.

The Second is that which is mutable only toward the good, so that that which is indeed good by its own nature can nevertheless turn out better. 

The Third is: that which, while indeed good by its nature, was nevertheless able to be changed both toward the good and from good toward evil. 

The first and the last of these three Classes are the extremes; the second, however, is the **natural middle** between them, through which the extremes are united. This middle partakes in both of the extremes and is therefore the most suitable and most proper middle: for it shares in one extreme—namely that it is changeable, specifically from good to a greater measure of good—as it also shares in the other extreme—namely that it is entirely immutable from good toward evil. 

And such a middle was necessarily required in the very nature of things; for otherwise a **Chasm** <term>Chasma: a wide gap or void in the chain of being that would prevent the higher from reaching the lower</term> would have remained, and one extreme would have been united with the other extreme without a middle, which is impossible and against the nature of things,

<meta>This page continues the logical refutation of the objection raised at the end of the previous page regarding the infinite divisibility of matter. The author is breaking down the term "actually divisible" to show it is a logical contradiction.</meta>

which Logicians call a **joining of things that cannot be joined** <note>original: "compositiones non componendorum"; a logical fallacy where two incompatible concepts are forced together.</note>, which is a combination of words or terms that imply a contradiction or an absurdity. This absurdity is hidden in this very term: ***Actually divisible***. This term suggests that one and the same thing is both divided and not divided at the same time. For the word ***Actually*** signifies an existing division, while ***divisible*** signifies not a division itself, but at least the capacity or potential by which something *could* be divided. This is just as absurd and contradictory as if someone were to say: ***visibly blind***, ***sensibly insensible***, or ***lively dead***.

However, if by the terms ***Actually divisible*** they do not mean two conflicting things, but only one—namely, that something is either truly divided already, or at the very least has the capacity to be divided—then the fallacy will easily reveal itself to us. 

First, if the phrase <note>original: "τὸ actualiter divisibile"</note> **"the actually divisible"** signifies nothing else to them than something that is already divided in this sense, then I grant the **Major premise** <note>In a formal logical argument (a syllogism), the Major Premise is the broad general rule or statement.</note>: namely, that whatever is truly divided as far as an actual division can possibly be made, is indeed divided into **indiscerptible** <term>indiscerptibiles: parts so small they cannot be further divided or torn apart; atoms.</term> parts. But by this same reasoning, the **minor premise** <note>The Minor Premise is the specific case being applied to the general rule.</note> is false: namely, the claim that matter is *actually* divided as far as actual division can possibly go. 

Secondly, if by what they call ***actually divisible*** they mean a thing that is only **divisible**—that is, something in which there is the **potential** <term>potentia: the inherent power or capacity to become something else, as opposed to "actuality."</term> or capacity so that it *could* be divided—then I now deny the major premise, namely that

Therefore, the nature and essence of God, as has already been shown in what precedes, is entirely **immutable** <note>Unchanging and incapable of change.</note>, as declared not only by Holy Scripture but also by our innate intellect <note>original: "connatus nobis intellectus"</note>, which has been implanted in our minds by God. Furthermore, if something progresses to a greater degree of Goodness, this happens entirely because of some greater being, in whose virtue and influence it participates. Now, however, no greater Being exists than God, and so he is in no way improved, nor can he become better, and much less can he decrease, which would imply imperfection. It remains manifest, therefore, that God, or the supreme Being, is entirely immutable.

...and continually to vary from one state into another.

1. There is, however, a twofold **mutability** <note>original: "mutabilitas"; the capacity for change or transformation</note>, one which has the power of changing itself either toward good or toward evil, and this is common to all creatures, but truly not to the **firstborn of all creatures** <note>This refers to the "Firstborn" or "Intermediary," a being like the Logos or Adam Kadmon who represents the first stage of creation.</note>. Therefore, a threefold <note>The text likely intended "threefold" (triplex) here, as it proceeds to list three classes.</note> **class of Beings** <note>original: "Entium classis"</note> is given here: 

**The First** is that which is entirely **immutable** <note>unchanging</note>. 

**The Second** is that which is changeable only toward the good, so that that which is indeed good by its nature may nevertheless become better. 

**The Third** is: that which, while it was good by its nature, could nevertheless be changed both toward the better and from good into evil. 

The first and the last of these three Classes are extremes; the **Second**, however, is a natural **medium** <note>An intermediary or bridge.</note> between them, through which the extremes are united. This medium participates in both of the extremes and is therefore the most convenient and most appropriate middle ground: for it participates in that extreme which is indeed changeable—namely, from good to a greater measure of good—as well as in the other extreme, which is entirely immutable from good to evil. 

Such a **medium** <term>intermediary <note>In this philosophical system, a "medium" is a necessary logical link that prevents a "gap" in the chain of existence between the infinite God and the finite, fallible world.</note></term> was necessarily required in the very nature of things, because otherwise there would have remained a **chasm** <note>original: "hasma," likely from the Greek "chasma," meaning a vast gap or void.</note>, and one extreme would have been united with the other extreme without a middle, which is impossible and against the nature of things.

Furthermore, all <term>innate notions</term> <note>original: "innatę notiones"; these are fundamental ideas or principles that scholars of this era believed all humans are born with, such as the basic laws of logic</note> and dictates of truth—which all people find within themselves—would be false, and consequently, so would any conclusions drawn from them.

For all true knowledge, and the certainty of our understanding, depends upon the truth of the objects themselves, which are also commonly called <term>objective truths</term> <note>original: "veritates objectivæ"; the reality of a thing as it exists in the world, independent of a person's thoughts or opinions</note>. In such a case, no statement could be immutably <note>unchangeably</note> true—not even those that are clearest and most obvious, such as: *the whole is greater than its part*, and: *two halves make a whole*.

It must indeed be granted that goodness is a great—nay, the greatest—cause of love, and its proper object. For the good cannot love the wicked, nor the wicked the good *as such* <note>original: "qua tales"; meaning in their specific capacity as wicked or good people.</note>; for there is no greater likeness than that which exists between one good thing and another.

Likewise, when one thing bestows Essence upon another—as when God and Christ give essence to their creatures (for from them alone does all true essence proceed)—there is similarly a certain likeness present. It does so in such a way that it does not adhere to the crystal, nor does it cause any <term>swelling</term> <note>original: "turgeſcentiam" — the author argues that if light were physical matter, it would cause the object it entered to physically expand or "puff up"</note> here, but rather through a certain intimate presence—because light is not a substance or a body, but mere action or motion. <meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into how light and motion pass through physical objects. It is therefore clear that motion can be transmitted through various bodies by another kind of penetration than any body or matter—no matter how subtle it may be—could achieve; namely, through <term>intimate presence</term> <note>original: "intimam præsentiam" — a philosophical concept where two things occupy the same "space" not by physical pores, but by a deeper, metaphysical connection where their natures overlap.</note>. If it can penetrate the bodies through which it passes by intimate presence, then it can be transmitted from one body to another in a single moment—or rather, it requires no time at all.

I would like it to be understood, however, that motion or action itself does not require time—not even the smallest amount—to be transmitted; although it is impossible for the body, in which the motion must be carried from place to place, not to require some amount of time, whether more or less, according to the type of body and the intensity of the motion that moves it.

Therefore we see how all motion and action, when considered abstractly, possesses within itself a wonderful subtlety or <term>spirituality</term> <note>original: "spiritualitatem" — used here to mean a non-material quality that transcends physical constraints like size and weight.</note> above all created substances, whatever they may be, such that neither place nor time can limit them. Yet they are nothing other than the <term>modes</term> <note>original: "modi" — in 17th-century philosophy, a "mode" is a state or quality of a substance (like its shape or speed) rather than a physical thing itself.</note> of created substances—specifically, their strength, power, and virtue—through which they can extend into great substances beyond what the substance itself could do alone.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of how motion and substance interact. And thus we can distinguish extension into <term>material extension</term> <note>original: "extensio materialis" — the physical volume or size that an object occupies.</note> and <term>virtual extension</term> <note>original: "extensio virtualis" — from the Latin "virtus" (power); this refers to the reach or sphere of influence of a being's power, rather than its physical bulk.</note>, which double extension every creature possesses. 

Material extension, then, is that which matter, the body, or the substance itself has, when setting aside all motion or action: and this extension, properly speaking, is neither greater nor smaller, while it always remains the same. Virtual extension is the motion or action which a creature has, whether given immediately by God, or received immediately from some fellow creature. Moreover, that which it has immediately from God (from whom it also has its essence) and which is the natural and proper effect of its essence, is more properly speaking the creature's own motion, because it proceeds from its inner parts: and therefore it can be called <term>internal motion</term>, to distinguish it from that external motion which is at least from another, and therefore in respect to the former can be called <term>foreign motion</term> <note>original: "motio peregrina" — an outside force that is "alien" to the object's natural state.</note>. 

And when the aforementioned external motion attempts to carry a body to a place or something toward which it does not incline by its own nature, then it is violent and <term>preternatural</term> <note>original: "praeternaturalis" — something that happens outside or against the normal laws of an object's nature.</note>: as when a stone is thrown upward into the air; this preternatural and violent motion is clearly local and mechanical and in no way vital, because it does not proceed from the life of the thing thus moved. However, any motion which proceeds from the proper life and will of a creature is <term>vital motion</term> <note>original: "motio vitalis" — motion driven by a soul or living force.</note>, and this I call the motion of life, which is not purely local and

But how motion or action can be transmitted from one body into another is a great question among many, because motion is certainly not a <term>substance</term> <note>original: "substantia" — in this context, a thing that exists on its own, like an object, rather than a quality of an object.</note> or a body; and if it is only the movement of a body, how can movement pass from its own proper subject into another? This is difficult because the very essence or <term>entity of a mode</term> <note>original: "entitas modi" — in philosophy, a "mode" is a quality (like "fast" or "red") that cannot exist without being attached to an object. It was a major debate whether a quality could "jump" from one object to another.</note> consists in this: that it adheres to or exists within its own body. 

Therefore, the response which seems best to me for this objection is this: that motion is not propagated from one body to another by <term>local motion</term> <note>original: "motione locali" — the physical movement of a thing from one place to another.</note>, because motion itself does not move, but rather it moves the body in which it is. And if motion were propagated by local motion, this motion would then be further propagated by another, and that again by another, and so on to infinity, which is absurd. Therefore, the manner of this propagation is through a real production or <term>creation</term>, so to speak; so that just as **God** and ***Christ*** alone can create the substance of any thing, while no creature [is able to] create or give entity...

## That common Philosophy treats [Angels] with too little subtlety; and that the Platonist concludes that Angels and spirits preceded [bodies], and will eventually succeed Bodies.

**Spaniard.** Your way of philosophizing favors the existence of spirits in some way, perhaps, but it does not favor their excellence and dignity. For how perversely does he think about immortal nature who proposes to us **incarnate and corporated Angels**, that is, those changed into Flesh and Body; and in turn, that Bodies are to be **Angelized** <note>original: *Angelizanda*</note> again (if I may use the term), that is, returned to the true substance of spirits? Does not anyone who imagines such conversions surpass even the monstrous fables of the poets' **Metamorphoses**? <note>A reference to the *Metamorphoses* by the Roman poet Ovid, a collection of myths about magical transformations which were often seen by philosophers as the opposite of logical reality.</note> He certainly undermines all the principles of sound **Metaphysics** <term>Metaphysics</term> <note>The branch of philosophy that studies the fundamental nature of reality, including the relationship between mind and matter, and between substance and attribute.</note> and reason.

**Frenchman.** On the contrary, the overturning of Metaphysical principles fits your teachers <note>The Frenchman is referring to the Scholastic "Doctors" or university professors who followed Aristotle.</note> rather than the Platonic ones. For how contradictory are the principles of the very concept that your teachers establish? How shallowly and with how little subtlety do they dispute concerning the inner essence of **Being**, and the uniqueness of lower beings? What do they reasonably reveal about the internal likeness of the **Creature** to the **Creator**, and about the primary distinction of each from the other? What do they say about the most inward difference between spirits and bodies? How un-ingeniously and with how little probability do they discuss the most famous **sin of the Angels**? <note>The "sin of the Angels" refers to the theological question of how perfect, spiritual beings like Lucifer could have chosen to fall from grace.</note> The Platonists certainly explain that matter—if not more truly—at least with more subtlety, fitness, and consistency.

### What Common Philosophy Says Concerning God

...it pleases me now to demonstrate, in passing, that this is against you.

Come then, step forward, and offer yourself to be run through <note>original: *confodiendum*; literally "to be stabbed," a rhetorical term for being defeated by one's own logic</note> by your own principles. Before you depart from me, you will be forced to confess entirely that *it is only through stupidity and ignorance that "Platonic atoms"—or intelligences reduced to a corporeal nature—can be accused of absurdity or impossibility.* Therefore, setting aside the truth of things as they actually exist <note>the *de facto* state of the world</note>, which I leave untouched, let us argue only about the possibility, suitability, and likelihood of things.

And first, I ask you: Could not God have created almost innumerable myriads of *intelligences* <term>Intelligences</term> <note>In this context, an "Intelligence" refers to a pure, non-physical spiritual being, often equated with an Angel in medieval and Renaissance philosophy.</note>*, that is, a certain incredible but nonetheless finite multitude of naturally Blessed beings, each of which possesses its own natural subsistence* <note>The ability to exist independently as an individual entity rather than just a part of something else</note>*; which may see itself directly insofar as it is visible, and most easily penetrate other Beings—that is, be able to reside in the very same location as them?* <note>The Frenchman is proposing a "spiritual physics" where spirits, unlike solid matter, can occupy the same space without clashing.</note> *Yet this would be in such a way that none of them is essentially equal to another, and many are therefore superior, and many likewise inferior; and finally, one exists that is by nature the most perfect of all, and one by nature the most imperfect.*

*I do not mean that it would be impossible for things even more perfect than that "most perfect" one, or more imperfect than that "most imperfect" one, to be produced; but rather that in actual fact, and in comparison with the beings that currently exist, this one would be the most perfect, and that one the most imperfect.*

# That common philosophy <note>original: *Phil. vulg.*, referring to *philosophia vulgaris* or the standard Scholastic philosophy taught in universities at the time.</note> has not very subtly exhausted its capability in eliciting consent, even though this consent is far thinner and more relaxed than the consent of a superior being.

## IV.

**The Frenchman.** I ask fourthly: is it not possible that the greatest part of these naturally blessed beings—having heard the exhortation of the First Intelligence <note>original: *primæ intelligentiæ*. ...as it occurs. This is because there is no being which, in itself and intrinsically, is not a natural, true, and substantial image of the Divinity, and which therefore, by the mere favor of God, cannot become a supernatural image of the same Divinity.

Furthermore, by the name *spirit*, we wish to signify the order of the most perfect things; by the name of *body*, we signify the class and order of highly imperfect things. *In our current state of affairs, <term>common philosophy</term> <note>original: *Phil. vulg.* or *philosophia vulgaris*. ### IX.

Furthermore, in Plato’s view, actual <term>impenetrability</term> <note>original: *impenetrabilitas*. ## That common philosophy lacks the subtlety to deny its own subsistence and substitute the divine in its place.

**The Frenchman.** Oh, what admirable cleverness you show in penetrating the doctrines of the Platonists! I will not object to you here—though it is a fundamental distinction—that a <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: *hypostasis*. In this philosophical context, it refers to the individual substance or the "personhood" that gives a being its distinct existence.</note> and another "hypostasis" are things similar to one another, differing only by a greater or lesser degree of perfection. They are certainly not repugnant to one another or diametrically opposed, as <term>penetrability</term> and <term>impenetrability</term> are contrary to each other. 

Instead, I offer this one response—or rather, the Platonists offer it: there is no created being for whom a divine subsistence, even if it is rightly called "supernatural," is not also most natural. For in Plato’s view, every creature requires a natural happiness, and moreover a divine or "supernatural" one: but it requires the first without delay, and the second to be granted through merit. 

Now, supernatural happiness is the most intimate union with God, the most perfect of all conceivable unions. For nothing is greater or better than the highest happiness; indeed, apart from the highest happiness, nothing is truly great or good, because happiness is the single measure of all greatness and goodness. Therefore, since according to the mind of the Platonists the highest happiness is this very perfect union with God, and since this highest happiness is required by every creature, they easily concluded that this union is also required, and that the creature...

### X.

Furthermore, it will seem incredible to future ages that Philosophers, who boast of their wonderful subtlety, have established the essence of the body and of corporeal nature in local <term>impenetrability</term> <note>original: *impenetrabilitate locali*. Namely, according to the mind of the <term>Scholastics</term> <note>Scholasticism was the dominant philosophical and theological system of the medieval schools, heavily influenced by Aristotle.</note>, matter penetrates form and form penetrates matter most perfectly, even though both are corporeal! And although you preach that those marvelous entities, which you manufacture everywhere and point out by the name of "accidents," are much more imperfect than your substances, you nevertheless [grant them that] <margin>as a property</margin> intimate, characteristic, and essential...

### *That Common Philosophy is insufficiently precise*

...that the spirit is confused with the body because of this; they wrongly boast that this is the characteristic glory of spirits. ### That the common philosophy treats this with little subtlety

I would grant that your thinkers argue more subtly, more conveniently, and more coherently than ours. For how does **Plato** not fight against reason—or rather, against himself—when he makes only the <term>Being of beings</term><note>original: "Ens entium" — a philosophical title for God as the source of all existence.</note>, or the supreme God, free from matter, but composes all other beings, whatever they may be and in whatever state they exist, out of *matter* and *form* or *idea*? How can "matter" properly belong to "intelligences"? <note>In this period, "intelligences" refers to purely spiritual beings, such as angels, who lack physical bodies.</note>

*Gallus*, if form as well as spirit, according to Plato, is nothing other than *light* or a *concept*; then surely matter, which is the opposite of form, is properly nothing other than the absence and negation of light or concept. But in any created being, no matter how intelligent, there is much more negation than light or concept; because it is a negation of infinite light or infinite concept, and is only a finite light or a limited concept. Therefore, in any created being, there is more *matter* than *form*.

Again, because those beings that have fallen into a sensible state <note>Meaning the physical world that can be perceived by the senses.</note> not only lack infinite light, but are also entirely deprived of that finite light which they naturally require, they are therefore, by a new title and a new reasoning, *material*. They alone are properly called *material* when they are compared with the blessed—the whole and naturally subsisting beings—just as those blessed beings are called the only *spiritual* and *immaterial* ones when they are compared not with God, but with wretched and sensible beings.

### That common philosophers reason with too little subtlety

Aristotle posited that while the earth was made of four elements (earth, water, air, fire), the heavens were made of a superior fifth substance.</note>, he did not mean the common stars nor the ordinary sky; but rather at times the pure **intelligible world** <note>The realm of ideas or spiritual realities that can be understood by the mind but not seen with the eyes.</note>; and at times even the sensible world (but not the whole of it, nor even any visible solid form of it, such as the stars visible to us). 

But [he meant] only that part of the sensible world which is most active—namely, the **thinnest spirits** <note>In early modern science, "spirits" were extremely subtle, fluid-like substances thought to carry life and motion through the body and the cosmos.</note> scattered throughout the entire machinery of the world, but especially visible in the sun and other stars, and also in souls. That the **Stagyrite** <note>A common nickname for Aristotle, who was born in the city of Stagira.</note> meant these spirits and not the common sky is proven by the most solid authors when they explain these words of his from Book 3 of *On the Generation of Animals*: <note>original Latin: "esse in universo animalem calorem, adeò ut quodammodo sint plena anima, unde consistant, statim atque ille excipitur."</note> *that there is in the universe a vital heat, so much so that in a certain way all things are full of soul, from which they consist as soon as that [heat] is received.* This is pure **Py-** <margin>thago-</margin> <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the word "Pythagorean" onto the next page.</note>

### On the philosophy of Angels.

...[This was the] opinion of the **Pythagoreans**, **Platonists**, and indeed of all the **Ancients**. Therefore, it is highly probable that **Aristotle**, by using the name *heaven*, understood the **intelligible world** <note>The realm of ideas or spiritual realities that can be understood by the mind but not seen with the eyes.</note>, while by the name *earth*, he almost always understood the **sensible world** <note>The physical world perceived through the senses.</note>, following the figurative language of the ancients. Furthermore, it is very likely that he recognized no other "eternity of the World" than that which was the eternity of **Pythagoras**, **Plato**, and all the ancients. This eternity is to be understood not as referring to the position or arrangement, nor even the present state of beings, but rather to individual beings themselves. Indeed, it is not even a "proper" eternity, but merely a very long duration.

It must be especially noted that when **Aristotle** interprets those words written in the *Phaedo* <note>One of Plato's most famous dialogues, depicting the final hours of Socrates and his arguments for the immortality of the soul.</note>—that *Socrates, having drunk the poison, would depart to the happiness of the Blessed; and that the Socrates who would be carried out or buried would not be [the real] Socrates*—when he interprets these words, I say, in such a way that *he concedes this regarding the mind, or the **active intellect** <term>active intellect</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "intellectus agens" is the part of the mind that makes thinking possible, often considered the only immortal part of a human being.</note>, but denies it regarding the soul*, he clearly shows that he follows **Plato’s** opinion concerning the dual state of beings: that of intelligibility and that of sensibility. 

For it is just as if he were to say that the individual beings from which Socrates is composed—subsisting by themselves—would be blessed; but that the imperfect and wretched **concretion** <term>concretion</term> <note>The temporary "bundling" or gathering of elements that forms a specific physical person or object.</note> of beings which is called "Socrates" or "Socrates’s soul" would not be subsisting or blessed in any way, except insofar as whatever is natural and positive within it is destined to endure for eternal time and be made blessed.

*That common philosophers are not sufficiently subtle*

To understand this, three things must be briefly observed. First, the exact same thing can designate opposites depending on what it is being compared to. For example, just as the **Jews**, when compared to the **Canaanites**, signify the *spirit*; yet when compared to **Christians**, they *mystically* <note>original: "mysticè"</note> signify the *flesh* <note>In early modern theological scholarship, "spirit" and "flesh" were often used as comparative ranks for spiritual maturity or the nature of religious law.</note>. In the same way, the word **soul**, when opposed to the **Body**, denotes the primeval and **intelligible** state of things <note>The realm of pure ideas and spiritual reality.</note>. However, that same word **soul**, when opposed to the **intellect**, represents a lower and **corporeal** <note>Physical or bodily.</note> state of things.

Second, when **Plato**—and **Aristotle** following Plato—speak with the greatest precision, they use the name **intellect** to designate beings that exist naturally, separately, and by themselves. By the name **soul**, however, they designate beings that are bound <note>The Latin "damnata" suggests being "sentenced" or restricted to the material world.</note> and which perceive in a most imperfect way through their mere totality. Nevertheless, because the name "intellect" is occasionally applied to the other state due to a certain similarity, and the name "soul" is likewise often applied to the first state, the same Philosophers sometimes use specific terms to avoid confusion. They call the first state either the **active intellect** <term>active intellect</term> <note>The part of the mind that actively produces thought and understanding.</note> or the **universal soul**. The second state they call either the **passible intellect** <term>passible intellect</term> <note>Also called the passive intellect; the part of the mind that receives impressions. The author notes that philosophers consider this state not to "act" in a true sense, but only to "undergo" or "suffer" impressions.</note> or the **particular soul**.

### *That Common Philosophy is Insufficiently Subtle*

Earlier in the same chapter, he praises the ancients for making **act prior to potency** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "act" (actuality) refers to something being fully realized or in motion, while "potency" (potentiality) is the mere capacity to become something. Usually, Aristotle argues that actuality is superior to potentiality.</note>, and specifically **Anaxagoras**, because he made **Mind** <note>original: *mentem*; referring to Anaxagoras’ concept of *Nous*, a cosmic intelligence that sets the universe in motion.</note> [prior]. However, when he himself elsewhere makes potency prior to act, he considers it **logically**, not **physically** <note>To consider something "logically" refers to how we define it or arrange it in our minds; to consider it "physically" refers to its actual existence and sequence in the natural world.</note>; or if he does consider it **physically**, he is not comparing the **intelligible state** <note>The realm of pure thought and spiritual beings.</note> with the **sensible state** <note>The physical world we experience through our senses.</note>. Rather, he is comparing the secondary notions of the intelligible state with the primary notions of that same state; and he compares the local motion of the sensible state with the **efficient principle** <note>The "efficient principle" or cause is the agent that brings a change about (e.g., a carpenter is the efficient cause of a table).</note> of that same motion.

Generally, those things stated **physically** by his predecessors, he refutes as if they had been stated **logically**; and against those things stated **logically**, he scoffs as if they had been argued **physically**. In this way, he refutes the things most divinely asserted by **Plato regarding the universal being prior to individuals** <note>Plato’s Theory of Forms suggests that the "Idea" (the Universal) of a thing is more real and exists before the specific physical objects (individuals) we see.</note>, treating them as if they were affirmed about a **logical universal** <note>A mental category used for classification, rather than a real, existing Form.</note>.

And conversely, those things which were prudently declared by the **Pythagoreans** regarding the substance of sensible things—taken in a popular, verbal, and **logical sense**—he scorns, treating them as if they were explained in a **physical sense**, concerning both **metaphysical (or intelligible)** and **physical (or sensible)** substance. He does this so much that in Chapter 5 of Book 1 of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: *Metaph.*</note>, he boastfully says that the Pythagoreans **acted very simply, because they defined things perfunctorie, and thought that whatever was first defined was the substance of the thing**. This he says despite it being clear that they sometimes spoke in a popular manner, but more often in a subtle and...

# That it is least reasonable

[...to be an ima]ge substantially immortal, endowed with intellect, intended to be made blessed by the singular enjoyment of the Divine, and finally independent of all matter, subjection, and created action; and yet, on the other hand, to be so degenerate, filthy, shameful, needy, and empty, that it essentially, absolutely, and by its own nature hungers for a body. *The Frenchman.* <note>The Frenchman likely represents the author’s own view, leaning toward Cartesian or modern philosophy.</note> Oh, what an excellent and subtle distinction! Do you not see that you are openly and entirely assuming the very point in question? For what is an **incomplete being** <term>incomplete being: *ens incompletum*, a being that cannot exist or function fully on its own, but must be joined to something else to form a whole</term> except a being deprived of its **natural subsistence** <term>subsistence: the ability of a thing to exist independently</term> and thus deprived of a comprehensive understanding of itself? 

Therefore, when you say that the union of incomplete beings prevents that which is "higher" from seeing itself and acting according to its immaterial nature, it is exactly as if you were to say: *beings that are deprived of their natural existence, understanding, and action are deprived of their natural existence, understanding, and action when they are united to beings that are similarly deprived.* This is clearly ridiculous; it offers the very claim you are trying to prove as the reason for the conclusion. Indeed, it is not the union that hinders understanding; rather, your argument assumes the understanding is already hindered by something else.

## That they declare it in a way that is least rational. Something which the Scholastics are by no means able to do.

->IV.<-

**Fourthly**, the more subtle authors of the <term>School</term> <note>Scholasticism: the dominant system of theological and philosophical teaching in medieval and early modern European universities, heavily based on Aristotle and the Church Fathers.</note> (such as Father Giattinus <note>Domenico Giattini (1596–1672), a Jesuit theologian and scientist.</note> and Suarez <note>Francisco Suárez (1548–1617), a highly influential Spanish Jesuit philosopher.</note>, who cite Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic philosopher.</note>, Part 1, Question 89, Article 1) eventually saw clearly that this requirement of union with the body is so irrational with respect to the soul that it would make the soul utterly insane if it were attributed to it for all time. Therefore, they decided it must be said that *this union is sought for only a certain time; and thus for only a certain time is our soul incomplete,* and thereafter it is perfectly complete.

This opinion of theirs, which immediately appears not only new, but even incredible and foolish in itself, they strive to strengthen with this plausible reasoning. *The rational soul,* they say, *is capable of two kinds of operations: for on one hand, it is able to produce sensations and propagate its own species <note>To "propagate its species" refers to biological reproduction.</note>, and on the other hand, it can understand. Therefore, lest either faculty be frustrated in its acts, it ought to undertake both kinds of operations: the imperfect ones in the first place and for a very short time, but the perfect ones in the second place and throughout all eternity.*

**The Frenchman.** <note>original: "Gallus"; a character in the dialogue, likely representing a more critical or "modern" philosophical voice challenging traditional Scholasticism.</note> I have indeed read these things more than once, but I have always considered them worthless <note>original: "flocci toties feci"; literally "valued them as a tuft of wool," a Latin idiom meaning to not care a straw about something.</note>, both for many reasons and especially because the logic of the distinction—which the **Holy Doctor** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority in Catholic Scholasticism.</note> brings forward as the opinion of others rather than his own—proves absolutely nothing. 

For, from the fact that **Creatures** are of a certain and determined species, it does not follow that inferior things are not contained within superior ones, just as they are in the supreme being <note>God.</note>. For instance, just because an ***ell*** <note>original: "ulna"; a historical unit of measurement roughly the length of a man’s arm.</note> is of a determined length, it does not follow that a ***palm***, a ***half-palm***, and so on—and all smaller measurements—are not contained within the ell, just as they are contained within immensity itself. Or, just as all numbers are of a certain species, it does not follow that smaller numbers are not encompassed within larger ones, just as they are in infinity. 

This comparison is even stronger against my opponent, because in the *First Part, Question 47, Article 2*, he <note>Aquinas</note> cites **Aristotle** to argue that *the forms of things are like numbers, in which the species are changed by the addition or subtraction of a unit.*

That ***St. Thomas*** understands this axiom not only regarding God, but regarding all superior beings in respect to inferior ones, is most clearly evident from this passage of his in the *First Part, Question 76, Article 6, Reply to the 1st objection*: ***A more perfect form contains by its power whatever belongs to the inferior forms***. ### VI.

Let us press the Scholastics <note>The Scholastics were medieval scholars and theologians who used a specific system of logic, often based on Aristotle, which dominated European universities.</note> even more forcefully with their own machines <note>original: "machinis" – here used as a metaphor for their own logical methods and tools</note>, and let us use nothing against these subtle men except "arguments directed at the person" <note>original: "argumentis ad hominem" – a strategy of using an opponent's own premises or character against them.</note>.

For in this way, the School proves that the ***form of fire*** is different from the ***form of water***, because the latter recovers its own coldness. Therefore, if the effects are different in species, the causes or forms are also different. Yet, in many men and women, we experience temperaments that are more than just different in species, and we see effects that are monstrously diverse. Certainly, a greater diversity of temperament shines forth among humans than between the temperaments of gold and silver, or an apple and a pear.

## VII.

**The Gaul.** But the principles of your Doctors <note>Referring to the "Doctors of the Church" or the Scholastic professors in universities.</note> do not in any way support the nobility and excellence of our souls. This is so that nobler dispositions demand a nobler form, and the nobler the dispositions are, the nobler the form they require; and conversely, a nobler form requires nobler dispositions. The more noble a form is, the more noble are the dispositions it requires—to such an extent that the same proportion exists between one set of dispositions and another as exists between one form and another.

### XII.

The **rational soul** <term>rational soul</term>, as the **School** <note>The "School" refers to Scholasticism, the dominant academic philosophy of the time, which blended Christian theology with Aristotelian logic.</note> describes it, cannot live through truly material sensations. Indeed, **Pope Agatho** <note>Agatho (Pope from 678–681) was central to the theological debate over the "two wills" of Christ; the author here uses his definitions to argue that different natures—divine/human or spirit/matter—have distinct ways of acting.</note> defines motion as the motion of the nature to which the motion belongs; and he states that humanity cannot live through the operations of God, nor God through the operations of the **Creature** <note>In this context, "Creature" refers to anything created by God, specifically human beings.</note>. **Hispanus.** What is this meaning of yours that is so deeply hidden and so foreign to common understanding?

For the entities of which the human mind consists, insofar as they exist in a state of **intelligibility** <note>In Platonic thought, the "intelligible" world refers to things understood by the intellect alone, such as abstract truths and forms, rather than the physical senses.</note>, are an ***indivisible, immortal, and unbegotten soul, capable of being created by God alone***; however, insofar as they are subject to a state of **sensibility** <note>The "sensible" world is the realm of physical matter perceived by our senses (sight, touch, etc.).</note>, they are a ***divisible, corruptible, and begotten soul***.

## Which is by no means reasonable

...strictly taken, to proceed from God alone. But because we are currently discussing the opinion of the Platonists rather than my own, I say that they held the same view regarding the soul's indivisibility as they did its <term>ingenerability</term> <note>The state of not being created or produced; being eternal and without a beginning.</note>: namely, that the rational soul, insofar as it is **intelligible** <note>Accessible only to the mind or intellect, rather than the physical senses.</note>, is in every way uncreated, indivisible, and immortal; but insofar as it is **sensible** <note>Related to physical sensation and the material world.</note>, it is created, divisible, and mortal.

That is, *in relation to many highly visible effects*, it is as if it lacked parts entirely and were completely **indissectible** <note>original: "insectilis"; something that cannot be cut or divided into smaller pieces.</note>. Perhaps **Augustine** would not entirely reject their explanation, since it is quite clear that the holy Doctor—if he were dealing with metaphysical indivisibility, or the soul *as it is in itself*—would not have doubted *whether the rational soul is generated through propagation* <note>original: "an Anima rationalis propagatione generetur." Furthermore, the holy Prelate offers this reason for his opinion: namely, that the furthest part of a plant cannot be touched without the whole body and the head itself...

*Gallus.* You are completely mistaken. # On the Rational Soul

...is more fitting. Indeed—even if one rejects the doctrines of the Academy <note>Referring to the Platonic Academy; Gallus is arguing that his view works even without relying on specific Platonic dogmas.</note> and preserves the nature of bodies (which are essentially blind and will never cease to be bodies)—you could have philosophized about our soul more solidly, more ingeniously, and more suitably for refuting the arguments of the impious.

**Spaniard.** How so?

**Gallus.** By asserting that, just as the soul is perfectly one (no differently than the whole Man is one), it is also truly twofold. That is to say, it is composed of two parts: one which is propagated through generation <note>original: "generatione"; meaning biological reproduction from parents.</note> and is mortal, and the other which is created anew by God alone and is immortal in its own right. Neither of these parts—if viewed absolutely and precisely on its own, setting aside all other assumptions—would strictly require the other. Nevertheless, given the current state of things, each of them seeks a mutual union both with the other part and with the body. Indeed, having formed the plan to raise His creatures to a supernatural height, God decreed *to deprive a certain order of <term>Beings: "Entia", here referring to spiritual or intellectual substances</term>—which are intermediate between the higher and the lower things, yet truly and properly intellectual by their own nature—of all natural action, life, subsistence, and happiness for a time. He decreed that He would not illuminate these individual Beings except through an intimate conjunction with a certain corporeal soul and with a certain body which is called "human"; and that through this kind of illumination, they would be led toward the highest [summit] of divine life...*

# That it is Least Reasonable <note>This heading continues a logical argument from the previous page regarding the nature of the soul.</note>

...and to lead to the merit of happiness. In turn, God has decreed that no body at all, or <term>corporeal spirit: "corporeus spiritus", refers to the "animal spirits" or biological energy that 17th-century thinkers believed animated the physical body</term>, can arrive at that glory and blessedness of which it is capable, unless it becomes a part of a human body or of a human's corporeal soul; and so, unless it is coupled through this body and soul with one of those intellectual beings <note>original: "entibus intellectualibus"; here meaning pure minds or spirits.</note>. 

With this assumed, it is most perfectly clear how the mind—which in man is individual and immortal—even though, viewed absolutely and with every assumption set aside, it would in no way need the body or bodily sensation, nor be required by them in turn, and through its own essence alone could naturally be most luminous, most blessed, and most perfect; nevertheless, in the present state of things, it essentially and intrinsically desires a union with the body and the corporeal soul, and this union in turn is essentially and intrinsically desired by the body and the corporeal soul. 

Indeed, there is nothing that every single <term>Being: "Ens", a general term for anything that exists</term> demands more intrinsically, more naturally, or more essentially than happiness—either natural happiness, or, if that is denied, supernatural happiness. This is because it properly demands happiness alone, while demanding all other things only for the sake of that one goal. Since, however, natural happiness is denied in the present state, and cannot be obtained except through supernatural happiness, and that only through the intimate connection of the mind with the body and the body with the mind; nothing is [demanded] more intrinsically, more naturally, and more essentially by both...

# ->Vivid Sketch<-

[...scraps] stained with filth, the wrappings of cobwebs, and finally, you will be stunned to find that what lies hidden here is the pure soot from countless oil lamps lit for the display.

In the same way, as long as the **Philosophy of the Schools** <note>The Scholastic system of the medieval and early modern universities, which favored logic and the works of Aristotle.</note> is explored from afar or from the outside—that is, from a distance or even from close by, yet still from an external vantage point—it appears admirable and consistent in every part. For that long, nothing seems more just, nothing more rational, and nothing more perfect. During that time, it distinguishes the Creator from the Creature, Spirit from Body, and **substance** from **accident**, <term>accident: <note>In this philosophy, a "substance" is a thing that exists by itself (like a tree), while an "accident" is a property that exists only in something else (like the greenness of the tree).</note></term> and indeed, complete substances from incomplete ones; it even distinguishes those incomplete substances produced by creation from those produced by **eduction**. <term>eduction: <note>The Scholastic theory that "forms" or natures are not created from nothing, but are "drawn out" or "brought forth" from the potential of matter.</note></term> Finally, for that long, it discriminates between qualities and quantity, and absolute qualities from **modal ones**, <term>modal qualities: <note>Refers to "modes," which are specific ways a quality exists—for example, the specific degree of heat rather than just the concept of heat itself.</note></term> and natural things from supernatural ones, using an admirable method.

Here you will find nothing but masks, nothing but illusions, nothing but clouds, nothing but smoke; you will find no certainty, no stability, and no light. Certainly, you will be unable to excuse your **Doctors** <note>The "Scholastic Doctors" or professors who were the ultimate authorities in the universities.</note> except by saying that they feed their students and followers with mere wordplay and mere wind. They explain nothing in reality, and even when they seem to establish something certain and determined, they nevertheless [establish] nothing certain...

# ->Common Philosophy<-

...they establish, determine nothing, and say only those things which, because of their vague and most general meaning, can be adapted equally to all the opinions of all philosophers.

Certainly no one, unless he is a blockhead <note>original: "stipes," literally a wooden log or stump.</note> or close to the stupidity of the common mob, will be content with these names of *accidents*, *qualities*, and *entities*, but will expect a further explanation.

2. ...that this belief about a soul or a spirit <note>original: "anima geniove"</note> can only convince the lowest minds; however, to those of even moderate intelligence, after a few moments of examination, such an idea does not even appear likely. Even if this new observer does not actually think any differently than the first or second groups <note>referring to the mechanists and the "soul" theorists mentioned on the previous page</note>, he nevertheless proclaims that he will explain everything in a far different and much easier way. Accordingly, he claims that the various and wonderful effects of clocks arise from multiple and various "qualities"—namely, from the **Tupinamboric**, the **Quoniambecan**, the **Margajutic**, and so on. <note>These nonsensical terms are derived from the names of indigenous Brazilian tribes (Tupinambá, etc.) found in 17th-century travel logs. The author uses them here to mock the way Scholastic philosophers invented "occult qualities" to explain things they didn't understand.</note> He says that the **Tupinamboric** are qualities that carry weight and produce straight downward motion; the **Quoniambecan** are qualities that rotate in various ways and circulate in many forms; and finally, the **Margajutic** are qualities that are variously "toothed," stopping, releasing, impelling, pulsing, pulling back, counting, and so forth.

Truly, if someone were to philosophize in this manner to the vast multitude of people who have not yet been taught the inner workings of a clock, he would undoubtedly be preferred over the first and second groups. He would be believed to be passing down more solid and well-perceived truths; and this one man would eventually have all those of moderate intelligence as his followers. Yet, it is certain that he differs from the first group in no other way than this: that he speaks confusedly and indeterminately about whatever the first group tried to say clearly and with certainty.

And yet, neither **Aristotle** nor the **Scholastics** <term>Scholastics: <note>Medieval and Early Modern university philosophers who relied heavily on Aristotelian logic and "hidden qualities" to explain nature.</note></term> have achieved anything else. **Plato**, **Pythagoras**, and others have provided nothing else but emblems...

...and the inventors of riddles offered more than what was offered by the others! Finally, nothing else was attempted by Democritus, Epicurus, and many who lived far before them, than what was attempted by those first thinkers who explained all things by *motion* and *figure* <note>In 17th-century physics, "figure" refers to the specific shape or geometry of particles.</note>.

But your Scholastics <term>Scholastics: Philosophers and theologians in medieval and early modern universities who relied heavily on Aristotle's logic and abstract definitions.</term>—these "excellent men," to be sure—supposed that Aristotle disagreed with both the second and the first groups. They did not see that the things said by Aristotle himself determine nothing; or rather, that they are certainly the mere dogmas of the Platonists, Pythagoreans, and Democritans, described not physically, but logically, or as you wrongly say, metaphysically. In the same way, the description of the wonderful effects of the clock *through the qualities* set out above <note>Referring to the nonsensical "Tupinamboric" and "Quoniambecan" qualities mentioned on page 241.</note> is not physical, but logical, or as you wrongly call it, metaphysical.

Truly, this description of the clock by qualities, however logical and very obscure it may be, and unworthy of a discerning man (being used only with the lowest or middle rank of minds), is nevertheless clearer, more certain, and in many respects more defining than all the definitions of bodies and bodily properties devised by the Scholastics.

For what, I ask, do the Scholastics bring forward besides the name of "quality," both in general and in particular? Indeed, to explain certain clearly wonderful phenomena of nature, they wrongly—in my judgment, at least—flee to "occult" <note>original: "occultas"</note> entities and qualities of I know not what kind. among the Scholastics <term>Scholastics: Philosophers in medieval and early modern universities who relied on formal logic and abstract definitions to explain the natural world.</term> there are "occult qualities"—or rather, every single quality is equally "occult" <note>original: *qualitates occultæ*; "Occult" here means "hidden" or "not directly observable," referring to properties like magnetism that the Scholastics could name but not explain mechanically.</note> to them. However, these "good men" call those qualities *occult* for which no name has yet been assigned; meanwhile, they call those things "known"—and truly believe them to be known—which are designated by some specific name. Suppose there existed a name that signified that action by which a magnet attracts iron and turns toward the pole as precisely as the name "heat" signifies that action by which fire twinges and pricks our bodies when brought close. Surely, the one quality and action would be just as "known" as the other, because the Scholastic would have no clearer a concept of the one than he has of the other.

In truth, the perceptions that the Scholastics actually acquire—whether concerning the various attractions and directions of the *magnet*, or concerning the powers of the *suckerfish* <note>original: *remora*; ancient and medieval writers believed this small fish could stop a ship in its tracks by attaching to its hull.</note>, the *electric ray* <note>original: *torpedo*; a fish known since antiquity for its ability to deliver an electric shock.</note>, and other bodies which they themselves call *occult qualities*—these perceptions, I say, do not differ from their other perceptions concerning the virtues of fire (for example) or ice, except for the fact that a specific name has been found to point out the latter externally, but not the former. If "gagos," "matras," and "paslas" <note>Nonsense words invented by the author to mock the arbitrary nature of Scholastic naming conventions.</note> were established to specifically signify the condition or property of the *electric ray* or the *suckerfish*, then surely, according to the Scholastic way of philosophizing, these would be no more "occult" than any other qualities among them; because...

**The Frenchman.** And yet, if from one side philosophy takes away <note>The Frenchman is responding to the Spaniard's previous claim that philosophy destroys faith.</note> religion, from the other side—by which it corrects the former—the philosophy of **Plato** introduces religion, prayers, sacrifices, and equally the fear and love of God. In that way, like the **Spear of Achilles** <note>original: *Lanceæ Achilleæ*. In Greek mythology, the spear of Achilles could heal the wounds it had previously inflicted. The Frenchman suggests that if philosophy causes spiritual doubt, the higher philosophy of Plato provides the cure.</note>, it heals the very wound it inflicts. It is certainly established that there has never been any sect that held a better account of morals, and indeed of piety. For where, I ask, does the chief concern of the Platonists tend, if not to urge moral men toward the study of virtue and the worship of Divinity? **Irenaeus** <note>Irenaeus of Lyons (2nd century AD), an early Church Father who, while critical of Gnosticism, often acknowledged the alignment of Platonic thought with Christian truths.</note> certainly makes Plato more religious than the others, and he has the rest of the Church Fathers in agreement on this point. 

But I would like you to observe what one of the more recent **Peripatetics** <note>original: *Peripateticis*. Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note>, **Gallutius** <note>Tarquinio Galluzzi (1574–1649), a prominent Jesuit scholar and commentator on Aristotle and Virgil.</note>, says. "**Plato**," he says in his *preface to the Ethics of Aristotle*, "composed the dialogue on virtue—that is, those ten volumes of the ***Republic***—the argument of which is that the impious, the unjust, and those estranged from God (even though they are commonly thought most religious and are most flourishing in wealth) are nevertheless to be considered the most unhappy, equally weighed down by every kind of trouble. On the contrary, those whom the common people call wretched and troubled—provided they are friends and favored by the Almighty God—are to be judged all the more happy because they are more exposed to fortune, and are held in greater hatred by the people on account of their right actions and public benefits." Now this seems to be the sum of all the **Sacred Scriptures**, and of that wisdom which was commended by the pronouncements of **Solomon** and made known by the most holy oracles.
