<header>Sketch of the Argument <note>original: "Hypotyposis." This is a Greek rhetorical term referring to a vivid, picturesque description or a summary outline of a subject.</note></header>

...with commendable practice, miraculous genius, and matchless eloquence, he sought, discovered, and brought [these things] to light.

Why say more? Did Plato not promise the coming of the Messiah? Is he not said to have described that heavenly Master—not merely as someone like himself, as the Hebrew Lawgiver <note>Moses, traditionally regarded as the author of the first five books of the Bible and the source of the Law.</note> did, but as one much more worthy than himself and superior to the human lot? Indeed, in the dialogue *On Prayer* <note>original: "de voto." This refers to the *Second Alcibiades*, a dialogue attributed to Plato in the Renaissance (though modern scholars doubt its authenticity) which discusses how humans should pray to the gods.</note>, after he inquired into what the true form of praying to God might be, he immediately responded: *A Master will come from heaven, who will teach all mortals the true way of worshipping and beseeching God.* And in the 4th book of the *Laws*: *It is right that God should offer himself to us as both the rule and the measure, and for that reason, a certain "God-man" will be born in some part of the world.* 

The sufferings of the coming Messiah are certainly prophesied so expressly in Book 2 of the *Republic* that hardly anything more distinct is found in the Book of Isaiah. <note>The author is comparing Plato's description of the "Just Man" to the "Suffering Servant" prophecies in Isaiah 53, a cornerstone of Christian messianic interpretation.</note> *The Just Man*, he says, *will be scourged; he will be tortured and suffer chains, etc., and finally, having endured all evils, he will be lifted up onto a cross.* <note>original: "in crucem tolletur." In the original Greek of the *Republic* (361e), Plato uses a word meaning "impaled," but Renaissance Christian translators frequently used "crucified" to strengthen the link to Jesus.</note> Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150 – c. 215 AD), an early Christian theologian who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Christian faith.</note> and Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260 – 339 AD), the "Father of Church History," who wrote extensively on how Greek thought prepared the way for the Gospel.</note> attest that this was spoken concerning Christ. 

Finally, as he was near death—as Rhodiginus <note>Caelius Rhodiginus (1450–1525), an Italian scholar known for his massive encyclopedia of ancient lore.</note> and Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the most influential Platonist of the Renaissance, who translated Plato's entire works into Latin.</note> report—he clearly confirmed what he had written in the dialogue *On Prayer* and the 4th book of the *Laws*. He warned that *his own teachings and reminders should be followed only until something more majestic and sacred shows itself in the world to open the secret fountains of truth; whom, as a leader [one should]...*

**The Frenchman**. And yet, while on one hand it removes [superstition], on the other—by which it corrects the former—the philosophy of **Plato** introduces religion, prayers, sacrifices, and the fear of God alongside love. In this way, like the **Spear of Achilles** <note>original: "Lanceae Achilleae." In Greek mythology, the spear of Achilles was said to be able to heal the very wounds it had inflicted; here, philosophy heals the doubts it raises.</note>, it heals the wound it deals. It is certainly well-established that no sect ever existed that held a higher regard for morals, and thus for piety. For where, I ask, does the primary care of the **Platonists** lead, if not to drive men toward the pursuit of virtue and the worship of the Divine? **Irenaeus** <note>St. Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202 AD), an early Church Father who often used Platonic concepts to explain Christian theology.</note> certainly renders Plato *more religious* than the others, and he has the agreement of the rest of the Fathers on this point. 

But I would have you observe what one of the more recent **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetici: followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy, so named for his habit of walking while teaching.</term>, **Galluzzi** <note>Tarquinio Galluzzi (1574–1649), a prominent Jesuit scholar and author of commentaries on classical philosophy.</note>, says: "*Plato*," he says in his preface to **Aristotle's** Ethics, "composed that Dialogue on virtue—that is, those ten volumes of the **Republic**—the argument of which is that the impious, the unjust, and those estranged from God, though they may be commonly thought most religious and flourish in wealth, must nonetheless be considered most unhappy, as they are overwhelmed by every kind of misery. 

On the contrary, those whom the common people call wretched and burdened—provided they are friends and pleasing to the Almighty God—are to be judged all the more happy the more they are exposed to the whims of fortune, and the more they are hated by the common folk for their righteous deeds and public service. Yet this seems to be the very essence of all Holy Scripture, and of that wisdom commended by the proverbs of **Solomon** and proclaimed by the most holy oracles."

->## Common Philosophy.<-

...[he] has treated <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's catchword "aper-", likely "aperuerit" (has uncovered/disclosed).</note>, while the other has neglected it; those who have philosophized more loftily about our mysteries ought to have claimed this one rather than that one for themselves. ### Sketch of Common Philosophy.

...they seem to speak most openly. Therefore, so that you might refute their hidden meanings, the study of **Platonic doctrine**—the most secret of all doctrines—is absolutely necessary for you.

***The Spaniard***: I, however, care very little what those insane scoundrels <note>original: "Nebulones"</note> thought, or rather, how they raved; and to this one thing at present I aspire: that I may comprehend, by subtle reason or whatever understanding possible, what is to be deeply held concerning the sacred mysteries of faith. Moreover, I hold it as certain that I can achieve this nowhere else than among our own theologians, who are easily the masters and leaders of all others. For what do your Doctors—whoever they may be and by whatever name they might boast—explain and teach until now concerning ***Grace*** and ***Predestination*** (which, by **Augustine’s** testimony, is the unique marrow of Christian wisdom), except what they have clearly learned from two Spanish heroes? <note>These "heroes" are Diego Álvarez (Dominican) and Luis de Molina (Jesuit), whose differing views on grace and free will sparked a massive theological debate in the late 16th century.</note> Indeed, what **Jerome** said of the **Arians** <note>Early Christians who believed Christ was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> as a reproach, we can affirm of our theologians as praise: for the entire orthodox world marvels that it is now also either an **ALVARIST** or a **MOLINIST**. <note>This is a clever reversal of St. Jerome’s famous remark, "The whole world groaned and marveled to find itself Arian." Here, the Spaniard boasts that the whole world now follows one of the two Spanish theological schools.</note>

***The Frenchman***: And yet, the refutation of common theology <note>term: "Theologia vulgaris" — This refers to the standard Scholastic theology taught in universities at the time, which the author is critiquing.</note> will demonstrate that your men have been, up to now, less theologians than philosophers; and that they deserve less praise for their treatment of ***Grace*** than for their illumination of ***Nature***.

# ON RECONCILING NECESSITY

Does God truly wish that we—who through that first crime became in some way like beasts of burden in his sight—should be freed from sin only through a blind, headlong persuasion, devoid of intellect, which is characteristic of Mules? ->**Of Faith with Reason:**<-

...is it such that it proposes nothing to be believed which, when accurately discussed, would appear foreign to reason, and which does not rather seem prudently believable by the light of manifest reason?

*The Spaniard.* Therefore, either the most holy Fathers <note>A reference to the "Church Fathers," the influential Christian theologians of the first few centuries.</note> deceive us, or they are certainly themselves deceived when they say that the whole wisdom of the Savior is like that **pillar of cloud** <note>In the Book of Exodus, a pillar of cloud guided the Israelites; it was light to the Hebrews but darkness to the pursuing Egyptians.</note>, which produces fire and splendor for the **Hebrews**—namely, for the little ones, the simple, and the ignorant minds—but creates darkness and gloom for the **Egyptians**—namely, for the "wise" and argumentative men? *The Frenchman.* As if indeed the supreme deity, whose essence is light, loves any but luminous and radiant shadows, or approves anything other than the **reasonable service** <note>original: "rationabile mentis obsequium," a reference to Romans 12:1, where Paul calls for a "reasonable" or "rational" sacrifice to God.</note> of the mind? Rather, one can hardly reach light more fittingly than through light, wisdom through wisdom, or reason through reason. By this very mark, according to the words of Christ, the good are discerned from the bad; and by this same mark, true dogmas are distinguished from false ones. For if **the evil one hates the light, lest his works be manifested** <note>A paraphrase of John 3:20: "For everyone who does evil hates the light... lest his deeds should be exposed."</note>, so a false **Religion** hates **Philosophy** and subtle reason, lest its glaring errors be uncovered. Just as the good love the light and walk openly with heads held high, so true mysteries do not seek out shadows, nor for themselves from the groves and... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; "groves" (lucorum) likely refers to the "sacred groves" used for hidden or pagan rites in antiquity.</note>

-># On the necessity of reconciling [faith and reason] <-

...horror of shadows; but they win veneration from the most shining brilliance of truth itself.

**The Spaniard.** As if indeed **Christian faith** <term>Christian faith</term> <note>original: "Christiana fides." In this context, the Spaniard argues that faith is a gift of grace that transcends human logic.</note> rests on human reason, and not only on **divine speech** <note>original: "divina locutio," referring to revelation or the Word of God as communicated to humanity.</note> and authority?

**The Frenchman.** Indeed, it rests on the **authority**, **wisdom**, and **truthfulness** of God speaking alone; but what, I ask you, is "divine speech"? For if you believe a matter most firmly on the basis of God's testimony alone—a matter which, when considering your own mind’s reasoning, is utterly uncertain and very obscure—then the testimony of God itself must be far more certain and manifest to you than the thing believed. For whoever believes a doubtful and plainly unknown thing on account of another thing that is either more doubtful, or equally doubtful or unknown, is most foolish.

**The Spaniard.** Divine speech is indeed most **certain**, but it is not, however, **evident**.

# On Harmonizing the Necessity [of Faith and Reason]

And now we seem to follow the authority of God <note>original: "Dei auctoritatem." In this context, it refers to the traditional justification for religious belief—that one believes because God has spoken.</note> whenever we follow reason itself and the motives upon which reason rests. This is because the whole of **divine speech** <term>divine speech</term> <note>original: "divina locutio." A theological concept referring to how God communicates truth to humans, whether through scripture, tradition, or natural reason.</note>—both as it exists in God and as it is received in man—is reason. That part of the divine speech which inheres in us is the very internal appearance of **credibility**; it is the fitting perception of arguments depending on either extrinsic or intrinsic **topics** <term>topics</term> <note>original: "locis." In classical rhetoric and logic, "topoi" or "places" are the sources or categories from which arguments are drawn.</note> which produce that credibility.

And so, as often as you say in your mind, *“I believe this thing because God has revealed it,”* you are saying this very same thing, but only in different words: *“I affirm this thing because a clearly perceived reason—persuaded either by miracles, etc., or deduced from the highest principles of Philosophy—convinces me to affirm it.”* For reason is, at least, the common and ordinary internal part of the divine speech, through which alone the other part of that divine speech <note>The "other part" likely refers to the external revelation, such as scripture or spoken prophecy.</note> becomes known to us.

Therefore, whoever opposes faith to all reason, and all reason to faith, acts just like one who opposes humanity to Christ, or the body to man. It is no more absurd to exclude humanity from Christ, or the body from man, than it is to exclude reason from faith; for Christ is no more intrinsically composed of humanity, and man of a body, than divine speech—and consequently faith—is forged from reason.

*The Spaniard.* <note>The "Hispanus" represents a dialogue partner in this philosophical exchange, likely taking a more traditional or skeptical view of the Frenchman's rationalism.</note> But you will never persuade me of such an incredible novelty, no matter what subtlety you might bring to bear on this matter. From this miserable success, it finally happened that these masked <term>sycophants</term> <note>original: "sycophantæ." In this context, it refers to deceptive informers or false accusers.</note>, insulting us as if we were dull and ignorant little men, possessed and boasted for a long time in the sacrilegious theft of a light that was not theirs.

But if Catholics, as they easily could have, had been instructed in the more secret discipline of the Philosophers and had turned the hurled weapons of reason back upon their Adversaries, then immediately all the splendor of those **Shadow-dwellers** <note>original: "Tenebrionum." Refers to those who operate in darkness or swindlers.</note> would have been changed into darkness. Those foolish fires <note>Will-o'-the-wisps or "ignis fatuus."</note> running along the riverbanks, or stars falling through the night air, would have been instantly extinguished. At the very least, they would have been held in no less contempt than those lowly little worms that glow at night, or certain pieces of rotten wood that shine among the shadows.

But while he truly erred in many matters, he was falsely accused of many more—and so furiously accused—that in order to calm the storm stirred up in the <term>Church</term> (at the hands of his enemies, though on his account), he voluntarily threw himself into the sea like another *Jonah* <note>Referring to the biblical prophet who was thrown overboard to calm a storm; here, it means Origen chose to stop writing to end the controversy.</note>; that is, he reduced himself by his own choice to a perpetual silence of both tongue and pen.

And then finally, having cast off his mask and laid aside the weapons of others, he at last put on his own weapons—weapons worthy of the *Prince of Darkness*—namely, ignorance and a contempt for reason. With these weapons indeed...

### On Reconciling the Necessity

...compared with unthinking beasts. Let there be, therefore, the **Eagle**, the **Ox**, and the **Lion** in the chariot of divine glory, but let there also be **Man**; or rather, Intelligence, under a human appearance, that is more than human. <note>The Eagle, Ox, Lion, and Man refer to the four living creatures in the visions of Ezekiel and Revelation, which the author uses here to symbolize different types of beings or faculties serving God.</note>

Therefore, in the future, let us be Jews to the Jews; but let us likewise become Greeks to the Greeks, Philosophers to Philosophers—and indeed, common Philosophers to the common, the mediocre to the mediocre, and the divine to the divine. This means that when we deal with the common people, who are unsuited for the hidden secrets of wisdom <note>original: "recondita sapientiæ arcana"</note>, we should act in a popular manner and disregard that most subtle reason which is strictly called reason. Indeed, that kind of Philosophy is no more suitable for "serpents" <note>likely referring to those of a low or worldly disposition</note> and base minds who still require "milk" <note>A biblical metaphor from 1 Corinthians 3:2, where "milk" represents basic teachings and "solid food" represents advanced wisdom.</note> than solid food is for infants; it is even treated as a plague. But if we see—as often happens—common spirits or men of average intellect stirred by excessive curiosity and aspiring higher than their capacity allows, we should by no means forbid them Philosophy (lest they struggle more obstinately toward what is forbidden), but we should instead usefully delude them. We should give them only words and, with innocent deceptions <note>original: "innocentibus præstigiis"; the author suggests using simplified language or "pious frauds" to keep the unlearned from confusing themselves with complex metaphysics.</note>, keep them away from the marrow [the essence] of things while appearing to lead them in. In this way, we may keep every person within their own rank.

But when we are outside the temple and the common pulpit, or away from the general assembly—when we write <term>theological treatises</term> <note>technical works discussing the nature of God and religious doctrine</note> for accomplished Masters, and when we deal with certain Persons of remarkable intelligence...

# On Reconciling Necessity #

...he is compared to foolish beasts. Therefore, let there be an **Eagle**, let there be an **Ox**, and let there be a **Lion** in the chariot of divine glory, but let there also be a **Man**; or an **Intelligence**, under the human form, that is more than human. <note>The author refers to the "Four Living Creatures" (the Tetramorph) from the visions of Ezekiel and Revelation, traditionally symbolizing the Evangelists. Therefore, in the future, let us indeed be Jews to the **Jews**; but let us likewise become Greeks to the **Greeks**, **Philosophers** to **Philosophers**—and indeed, common Philosophers to the common ones, mediocre to the mediocre, and divine to the divine. That is to say, when dealing with the common people who are unsuited for the hidden secrets of wisdom, let us act in a popular manner and reject that most subtle reasoning which is properly called "reason." For that kind of Philosophy is like poison and plague to those "serpentine" and lowest minds who still require milk, just as bread and solid food are unsuitable for infants. <note>This draws on the biblical metaphor from 1 Corinthians 3:2, suggesting that deep philosophical "meat" is dangerous for those who can only digest the "milk" of simple faith.</note>

But if we see—as happens quite often—common spirits or men of mediocre subtlety stirred by excessive curiosity and aspiring higher than their grasp allows, let us by no means forbid **Philosophy**, lest they strive all the more obstinately for what is forbidden. Instead, let us usefully play with them: let us give them only words, and by innocent deceptions, under the guise of introducing them, keep them away from the "marrow" <note>original: "medullâ." This refers to the inner essence or the deep, hidden truth of a subject.</note> of things; and in this way, let us keep everyone in their proper rank.

But when we discuss matters outside the temple and the popular pulpit, or away from the common assembly—when we write **Theological treatises** for accomplished Masters, or when we encounter certain people of a marvelous intelligence...

### Of Faith with Reason.

Would anyone want *Christ* to practice the trade of a carpenter, a tailor, a shoemaker, a baker, or a <term>tent-maker</term> <note>original: "scenofactoriam" — This refers to the craft of St. Paul, who made tents to support his ministry</note>? Finally, *Philosophy* is far less dangerous to men dedicated to *Christ* than *Money* is. Therefore, even if the *Church* were deprived of all riches and all external brilliance, power, and secular apparatus, it should not for that reason be destitute of the splendors and assistance of *Philosophy*.

Indeed, that famous <term>Apostate, Julian</term> <note>Julian the Apostate (ruled 361–363 AD) was the last pagan Roman Emperor; he attempted to revive traditional Roman religion and undermine Christianity</note>, who first despoiled the *Christians* of all their goods on the pretext that neither the first *Christians* nor *Christ* himself possessed anything, and that he wished nothing to be possessed by his *Disciples*; that same *Julian* forbade the study of humane letters and especially the study of *Philosophy* to *Christians*. # On the Necessity of Reconciliation

...for he wished <note>This sentence completes the thought from the previous page regarding Christ's choice of disciples</note> the truth to be revealed only to little ones, the simple, infants, or those like infants. Yet it is certain that Popes, Kings, and many others powerful in wealth are true disciples of *Christ*. Indeed, it is certain that not a few gain the heavenly kingdom through their riches; for if these same people were oppressed by poverty, they might be driven headlong to hell by desperation, impatience, or the compulsion of necessity toward every horrible crime, and from those crimes to the underworld. 

How much more certain is it then that many are led to the faith through *Philosophy* along with <term>St. Justin</term> <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD) was a philosopher who converted to Christianity and argued that any truth found by pagan philosophers was actually a gift from the "Logos" (the Word/Christ)</note>, who, if they possessed no understanding of things, would be most prone either to ridiculous superstitions or to absolute impiety and the mockery of all *Faith*? Furthermore, a certain wondrous thing can be observed in the later monsters of heresy. For what <term>Julian the Apostate</term> <note>The Roman Emperor who tried to dismantle Christianity by banning Christians from teaching or learning classical literature</note> strove for, the later heretics also attempted: and those who first condemned the riches of the *Church* were also the first to strip reason from *Christians*... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "exu-", likely intended to be "exuere," meaning to strip or divest</note>

Nor should it be thought because of this that the Church is opposed to itself, or its customs to its own customs. In fact, both the ancient and the modern state of the Church confirm what *Christ* prophesied when He was near death: *Amen, amen, I say to you, that you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; and you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy, and your joy no man shall take from you* <note>original: "Amen amen dico vobis, quia plorabitis, & flebitis vos..." — A quotation from the Gospel of John 16:20–22.</note>. From the death of *Christ* until Constantine, the Church wept and lamented; *Unbelief* (which to *Christ* is "the world") triumphed and rejoiced. But through Constantine, the Church’s sadness, mourning, and subjection were turned into joy, light, and dominion. The prior state of the Church, as I said above, corresponds to the mortal life; the latter corresponds to the immortal life of the *Savior*.

# Of the necessity to be reconciled

The former expresses the suffering Christ, the latter the rising Christ. In the former, Christ is born in the middle of the night and dies with the sun darkened: only a nightly flame guided the Shepherds, and only a star led the Kings to Christ; finally, only the *darkness made over the entire earth* <note>original: "tenebræ per universam terram factæ"; a reference to the eclipse during the Crucifixion described in Luke 23:44.</note> illuminated the Centurion <note>The Roman officer at the foot of the cross who, seeing the darkness and Christ's death, declared Him the Son of God.</note>: for only the more imperfect motives and the less sublime reasons were preached in that first state. While these points are indeed sufficient for convincing, many even stronger arguments remain. And first indeed, since Christ came so specifically and almost so uniquely for the sake of the Jews—to the point that when invited to illuminate the Gentiles <note>Non-Jewish peoples.</note> and certain of their future conversion (if He were to go to them), He answered publicly and openly *that He had not come except for the sheep that had perished from Israel* <note>original: "se non venisse nisi ad oves quæ perierant ex Israël"; a reference to Matthew 15:24.</note>—nor, if the Jews had listened readily, would the Apostles have first taught the Pagans...

...way <note>original: "-ria"; completing the word "contraria" or "opposite way" from the previous page.</note>, He did not wish to immediately make His own followers into **Philosophers** by some new and unusual miracle, and He declined to do so for various reasons. Furthermore, the Gentiles were to be promised a participation not only in the same grace, but also in the same assistance and means.

This was especially necessary as long as the first Leaders of the **Church** were **Jews**, since they traveled to distant nations for the sake of their fellow-countrymen <note>The "Diaspora," or Jewish communities living outside of Israel.</note> dwelling everywhere, and they devoted their primary efforts to them throughout their entire lives. It certainly cannot be denied that the first Fathers of the Church, the Apostles (all of whom, it is well known, were **Hebrews**), for as long as they lived, were quite reluctant to admit anything that might make them appear less holy, or even profane, to the Jews. Third, the **Gentile People**, who were far more numerous than the wise, and who—like the Jews—were men of a character... <meta>catchword: je-</meta>

# Of Faith with Reason <note>original: "Fidei cum ratione."</note>

...to be their custom. For in this way, an incredible weight of certainty attaches itself to the faith of Christ, once our own reason is taken into account. Indeed, hardly any room for doubt remains when a person sees, on one hand, that neither Christ devoted any effort to philosophy, nor were his disciples even slightly steeped in it. Rather, for nearly ten centuries, they seemed to shrink from it so much that they allowed it to be openly claimed, with almost unanimous prejudice, that *faith and philosophy do not agree*. 

And yet, on the other hand, that same person observes all the mysteries of the Christian faith—even as they were explained by Councils and Church Fathers <note>The influential theologians and bishops of the early Church.</note> who were for the most part unlearned in philosophy. The more deeply these mysteries are discussed and, as it were, "gutted" <note>original: "eviscerantur"; to examine something so thoroughly that its inner workings are laid bare.</note> for study, the more certain, clear, and obvious they appear, and the more they seem to align with the most general wisdom. 

Surely such a marvelous harmony could not have happened by chance. Therefore, since it by no means proceeded from human wisdom, one must confess that it originated from another source. *Therefore, this was the work of God*; it is not merely the "finger of God" <note>A biblical metaphor for God's direct intervention, as seen in Exodus 8:19.</note> at work here, but the entire "right hand of the Most High" <note>A phrase indicating God's full power and strength.</note>. It is not just the right hand, but the entire design of an infinite Mind that is present here. 

Consequently, that neglect of philosophy which was very useful and almost necessary at the beginning would today be quite harmful (considering those men who possess outstanding talent). Much less should it have been joined in an intimate bond with the holier mysteries of Christ; rather, it was necessary that it first be crushed...

<page-num>298</page-num>

### On Reconciling Necessity

...nearer <note>original: "ciniorem," likely a fragment of "viciniorem"</note>; but in that light you will notice no figure of trees, or meadows, or men. Why is this, you will ask? Do the <term>images<note>Original Latin: *species*. In early modern science, "species" were the "sensible likenesses" or "forms" cast by objects that traveled through the air to reach the eye or a surface.</note></term> no longer reach the paper? On the contrary, they reach it in far greater abundance, because the paper is then both more directly facing the objects and much closer than before. Therefore, these images rush in together with the light; but they are not separated, they are not unfolded, but remain contracted and entangled as they are poured around. This is why you see nothing on the paper while it is closer to the hole. But move it away little by little; the further you move it toward the opposite wall, the more clearly and distinctly you will behold the likenesses of the objects.

Behold for yourself an excellent symbol of the Christian faith! The Apostles and the first Fathers were closer to Christ, who is called the *Light* <note>John 8:12: "I am the light of the world."</note> because of his divinity, and the *Door* <note>John 10:9: "I am the door."</note> because of his humanity in the Gospel; indeed, he is even called the *Opening* <note>Original Latin: *foramen*. This refers to Song of Solomon 2:14, "in the clefts [foraminibus] of the rock," often interpreted by theologians as the wounds of Christ or the entry point of divine revelation.</note> in the Song of Songs. We, however, like the wall on the opposite side, are further removed from that light, that door, and that opening than the Apostles were. Consequently, there is a greater, denser, and more abundant light in the Apostles than in us: a stronger impression of universal principles flourishes in them than in us, but there is nonetheless a far smaller distinction of details in them than in us, and conversely, a greater confusion exists. For indeed, the further the **Church** has proceeded, the more unfolded a knowledge of the mysteries it has attained: and the further it progresses into the future, the more distinct a perception of truths it will acquire.

...is it necessary? # On Reconciling Necessity

...a part of the divine work which the Jews, for many reasons—owing to their innate lowliness, dejection, and laziness—were unable to reach. Out of His fatherly goodness, God violated the laws of His **common providence** <note>The "ordinary" way God governs the world through natural laws and cause-and-effect, rather than miracles</note>, which are the most glorious of all for us, for the sake of a people who were hardly capable of such great glory.

Similarly (though for other reasons mentioned previously), the use of **extraordinary providence** <note>Miracles or direct divine interventions that bypass natural laws</note> rather than ordinary providence was suitable for the first Christians. In contrast to the rule of common providence, this brings us more glory—and not just glory, but also greater practical benefit in the present. For since the entire business of divine providence concerning us revolves around free human *cooperation*, it is entirely fitting that God should bind the greatest rewards to this human effort when joined with the divine. Therefore, to stir up human diligence and industry, He clearly decreed: *to crown nothing with the beauty of supreme perfection or eternity that is not coupled with the highest care, labor, study, and skill of mortals.*

Thus, through the warlike virtue of **Saul** and **David**, God bestowed greater glory and more extensive rule upon the Hebrews than through all the wonders <note>Latin: *prodigia*, referring to supernatural signs or miracles</note> of **Moses**, **Joshua**, **Samson**, and **Gideon**. Likewise, through the single wisdom of **Solomon**, God made His people more illustrious among foreign nations and happier at home than through all the holiness of **Samuel**. For what kind of fruit, I ask you, comes from the victories of **Moses**, **Joshua**, and **Gideon**...

From this you see that the faith which **Philosophy** brings forth is more intelligible—and certainly less based on the senses—than that which is produced by any other motives.

->### Of Faith with Reason<-

...already, and thus contains human reason. Moreover, just as it is true in a certain sense that a man is not mortal and corporeal, but rather immortal and incorporeal—both because he is not purely mortal or corporeal, and because he is ***principally*** immortal and incorporeal—and just as it is likewise true that Christ is not a man, but God—both because he is not a mere man, and because he is ***principally*** God—it is in this same sense that it can be said that ***a Christian is a person of faith, not of reason.*** 

For this reason, Augustine intends only that Christians should not be seen as remarkable because of their reason alone (as if it were their chief ornament). Instead, they are to be preferred over all other men—even the most upright and those acting with the greatest wisdom—because of that prudent act by which they firmly cling to Christ. I have not been here to defend the opinion of *Jansenius* <note>Cornelius Jansen (1585–1638) was a bishop whose writings on grace and predestination sparked the "Jansenist" controversy. His views were often seen as too close to Calvinism by his detractors.</note> (which I entirely disapprove of), but merely for the sake of testing your wit. 

For it is clearly evident to *me* that your *theologians* are not followers of a theology that is argumentative, profound, subtle, or capable of gutting complex questions <note>original: "quæstionum exenteratricis"</note>—in short, not followers of scholastic theology—but are instead practitioners of a theology that is merely "positive," purely superficial <note>original: "cicatricis," likely used here to mean "scary" or "surface-level," implying they only see the outward marks of a text rather than its depth.</note>, and literal <term>textuariæ<gloss>a "textualist" approach that relies strictly on quoting authorities and scripture without applying logical or philosophical analysis</gloss></term>. Therefore, it was with the greatest indignation that I heard what was boasted by *you* in *my* presence yesterday: that it is the particular glory of your *Frenchmen* to join philosophy with *theology*. 

Indeed, I did not deign at that time to refute that opinion of yours regarding *your own people*—an opinion so far removed even from probability—but instead, intending to provoke the *French* fury in *you*, and ready to mock the simplicity or dullness of your *theologians* through your own person, I immediately pronounced that *theology* should have nothing in common with *philosophy*. I claimed that *your people* ought to be blamed for the very thing you praised them for, and moreover, I promised I would demonstrate this today. 

But since, from the answers you have given so far, you seem to be an adversary not at all unworthy of a *Spaniard*, and it appears that the victory to be won over *you* will not be without honor, I am now pleased to battle with *you* in earnest, 

<summary>The Spaniard reveals that his previous arguments were a test of the Frenchman's wit and insults the French school of theology as being superficial and "textualist" compared to the rigorous Spanish Scholastic tradition.</summary>

### On the necessity of reconciling Faith with Reason ###

...to recognize <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing a verb from the previous page such as *propugnare* (to defend) or *designare* (to designate).</note>, and to distinguish You with the glory of such an honorable defeat.

I confess, therefore, that faith must be joined with reason; but at the same time I maintain that such a <term>concord<gloss>original: "concordiam," the harmonious reconciliation between religious dogma and logical inquiry</gloss></term> cannot be established more subtly by anyone other than the Spaniards, and accordingly, no philosophy should be deservedly preferred over our own.

*The Frenchman*: Regarding this matter, if it pleases you, we shall discuss it more conveniently tomorrow.

-> THE END <-
